The Final Frontier: South African Space Agency

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
When you think of space, you think of Russia or America, think again. South Africa has had a space agency for 50yrs and we aren't just looking at the stars, but seeing what space can do for us!

Unique Selling Point:
Gladys Magagula is head of South Africa's mission control room at SANSA (South African Space Agency). She has seen us enter the space race in terms of satellite communication. Because of our prime position relative to space and weather conditions, South Africa is the communications choice for the USA, Russia and China. So much so, we were a part of the Apollo missions securing communication between South Africa and Houston's mission control, we transmitted "One small step for man, one giant leap for mankind." But we have continued and made the space communication race our own. We have sent 3 satellites into space and have had successful launches (from other countries). The information from these is priceless - we can see South Africa in a different way - from weather (droughts etc) and land surveying we can see EVERYTHING from space. So not only are we making money from communicating with satellites for other countries, we are also exploring and making our own satellites.

Summary:
We'll speak to a team of young black researchers who went to Antarctica for SANSA and what they did there and why it's so important to have a "hub" there.
We will also interview the head of the weather department Mpho Tshisaphungo - she'll explain operation Phakisa and how we are using the information to accurately forecast unexpected weather - like droughts and floods. They have information dating back 50 years and can spot trends and problems.

Further information:
The visuals are amazing!

Press Release:


SA Space Agency
Space Communication is a multi-billion dollar industry. And South Africa has joined the race to get satellites into space. Not only that, but we play a crucial role in facilitating satellite communication for the world, also monitoring natural disasters, climate change and more. Carte Blanche finds out why South Africa’s Space Agency has become integral to keeping the planet connected.


Script:


Neil Armstrong: “One small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.”
These iconic words uttered on the moon during the 1969 landing were actually transmitted to Houston’s mission control via NASAs satellite communications hub in South Africa.
Link: WHEN ONE THINKS OF SPACE EXPLORATION BEING THE NEXT FRONTIER, WE THINK OF NASA OR THE EUROPEAN SPACE AGENCY OR THE RUSSIANS OR THE CHINESE, NOT MANY PEOPLE KNOW WE HAVE OUR OWN, WELL WE DO, BUT NOT ONLY THAT, THE SOUTH AFRICAN NATIONAL SPACE AGENCY IS ONE OF THE MOST IMPORTANT IN THE WORLD.
Our geographical location in the Southern Hemisphere allows us to uniquely facilitate communications between earth and the worlds’ satellites.
Rocket launch: “On October 7, 1957, the US and the rest of the world were greeted by the sounds of Sputnik one.”
The following year NASA set up a South African satellite tracking facility, so that the Americans could communicate with - their satellite Explora 1-when it left the reaches of their airspace. Since then we have been integral to fuelling the space race with our two facilities in Hartbeeshoek – The Radio Astronomy Observatory which focuses on mapping our night skies and our space agency which has propelled South Africa forward into the satellite communication era - with technology that assists our cellphones, wifi, or GPS.
Link: SANSA’S HARTEBEESTHOEK FACILITY IS PART OF AN INTERNATIONAL NETWORK OF GROUND STATIONS THAT HOUSE ANTENNA LIKE ON THIS DISH THAT COMMUNICATEWITH THE SATTELITES ORBITING THE EARTH.
Welcome to the Antenna Farm. By tracking satellites for other countries or hosting their dishes, SANSA generates income. Gladys Magagula is currently SANSAs project manager.
Gladys: “During a satellite overpass, when it passes over our air space and when we can communicate with the satellite, I need to check the health status of the satellite in order to be able to continue; otherwise we lose the entire mission.”
In 2009 she was head of Mission Control. Her mission? To launch SumbandilaSat, a SOUTH AFRICAN earth observation satellite, into orbit.
Gladys: “Programming the satellite to do what, when and how, that’s what mission control is.”
Bongani: “So you are the head lady in charge?”
Gladys: “I hold the title undisputed, until maybe we launch the next satellite.”
Looking up at the night sky from rural Mpumalanga, Gladys never imaged she’d one-day be a mission control specialist.
Gladys: “It was an opportunity to see the world from sitting here.
Bongani: “Well you’ve seen a lot more than just the world?”
Gladys: “Maybe the universe.”
Engineer, Anthony Mokgolo, is chief technician of operations at SANSA.
Anthony: “I basically operate the systems, which is telemetry tracking and command, the satellites are continuously moving, orbiting the earth, so we need to position, our antenna’s in sight with the satellites in space and then we move with them as they are passing by Africa.”
Bongani: So if the aliens arrive, you’ll be one of the first guys who’d know?
Anthony: “I’d be telling you.”
SANSA were meant to track the new SPACEX rocket, owned by Elon Musk. Sadly, this was not to be. The satellite onboard would have supplied internet to African nations.
Gladys: “SpaceX rocket that exploded on the launch pad, it was a blow for us. It just goes to show, how risky the space business is.”
TIMELAPSE 3 seconds
SANSA monitored NASAs Orbiting Carbon Observatory -2 Satellite.
Gladys: “We helped with the beak off... HBK because the international community can’t pronounce it properly.”
Link: SO INSIDE THERE, IS MISSION CONTROL, THAT’S THE NERVE CENTRE OF THE FACILITY, ITS WHERE THE ANNTENNA THAT COMMUNICATE WITH THE SATELLITES ARE OPERATED FROM. IT’S ALSO A NATIONAL KEY POINT WHICH MEANS WE ARE NOT ALLOWED TO GO AND FILM...BECAUSE BIG BROTHER IS WATCHING.
There are over 1100 active satellites orbiting the earth taking photos like this one. Captured by SumbandilaSAT, it shows the agriculture surrounding Bloemfontein. Satellites have a range of applications - from military use to mapping crop growth for food security.
Clement: “We develop applications and products that help professionals to make better decisions, using satellite imagery.
Earth Observation Scientist Clement Adjorlolo compiles the mosaic of images which are then stitched together...
Clement: “We derive information from the satellite imagery to assist agriculture in terms of monitoring crop health and crop condition.”
SANSA captures the images which are then interpreted and can be used to make predictions – like the current drought which they predicted 3 years ago.
Clement: “We are able to give an indication as to what would be the condition for the forthcoming season, for instance, are we heading into a very dry season, or conditions will be normal?”
Another fundamental application is to observe our water supply.
Clement: “Satellite imagery also can be used to quantify the amount of water available. We can use satellite images to quantify algae bloom in the dam.”
The toxic blue-green algae shows up green on this image of Hartbeespoort dam. This vital information was then sent to the department of water affairs. Satellite technology like this is also used to track climate change like in the Southern Marion islands or map population sizes in cities like Cape Town where urban planning in necessary for growth.
Clement: “We are facing a number of socio-economic challenges that requires us to provide crucial information that goes to the extent of saving lives.”
SANSAs satellites have been used to track and monitor natural disasters like the Limpopo floods Or the devastation of burn scars left behind by fires, afterwards even the recovery of the vegetation can be monitored.
TIMELAPSE 3 SECONDS
SANSAs budget is relatively small – only R125 million of this years’ R7.4 billion department budget. But is the information SANSA is providing being used optimally when space technology is so useful?
Clement: “I would say to a large extent the data is being used. I’m not sure if the nation is aware to what extent it’s being used.”
SANSA wants to inspire the younger generation – people like Anthony - to reach for the skies.
Anthony: “The universe, the galaxies, the stars, we need to know them we need to understand what is actually beyond our borders.”
He was sent to SANSAs base in Antarctica, an ideal location to study space weather, as it’s where all the Earth’s magnetic field lines converge. Measuring the polarity is integral in understanding how we are protected from the suns solar flares, this information is then sent to SANSAs monitoring lab in Hermanus.
Anthony: “That is one highlight of my life!
Bongani: “Anthony, we’re black guys, we stay away from places like that.”
Anthony: “Hey, Black men cannot survive the cold. I actually wanted to show, hey I’m doing this.”
It was a 3 month trip he’ll never forget.
Anthony: “It’s a two week voyage to Antarctica, the deep blue sees they keep your seasick the whole time, one night I realized there was no longer darkness outside, we were only seeing light 24.7, and then it was cold! Take your deep freezer and then multiply it by 5-10.”
Anthony updated SANSAs space weather monitoring equipment and installed software that will assist the satellites in communicating better with their Hartebeeshoek facility.
Gladys hopes research trips like this will inspire our youngsters to become excited about space technology.
Bongani: “Why does South Africa need a space agency?”
Glays: “We depend a lot on space technology, not only as a country, but as human kind. We are not looking into sending someone to the moon as yet – maybe in the near future.”
The unfathomable distances of the unexplored universe make us contemplate our existence. It is a wonderful and immense engine that we still know very little about, and the space technology SANSA is using can only enhance our lives here on earth.


PROMO 1: 10 SECONDER
Neil Armstrong: “One small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.”
WHAT MAKES SOUTH AFRICA’S SPACE AGENCY INTEGRAL TO THE SPACE COMMUNICATION RACE?
PROMO 2: 15 SECONDER
Gladys: “We are not looking into sending someone to the moon as yet – maybe in the near future.”
WHAT MAKES SOUTH AFRICA’S VERY OWN SPACE AGENCY INTEGRAL TO FACILITATING THE TECHNOLOGY THAT KEEPS THE PLANET CONNECTED?

PROMO 3: 15 SECONDER
SOUTH AFRICA’S VERY OWN SPACE AGENCY FACILITATES GLOBAL COMMUNICATION WITH OUTER SPACE AND ALSO MONITORS NATURAL DISASTERS, GLOBAL WATER SUPPLIES AND CLIMATE CHANGE. MEET OUT SCIENTISTS FUELLING THE FAST-PACED GLOBAL SPACE RACE?

Clement: “We derive information from the satellite imagery to assist agriculture in terms of monitoring crop health and crop condition.” SANSA captures the images which are then interpreted and can be used to make predictions – like the current drought which they predicted 3 years ago. Clement: “We are able to give an indication as to what would be the condition for the forthcoming season, for instance, are we heading into a very dry season, or conditions will be normal?” Another fundamental application is to observe our water supply. Clement: “Satellite imagery also can be used to quantify the amount of water available. We can use satellite images to quantify algae bloom in the dam.” The toxic blue-green algae shows up green on this image of Hartbeespoort dam. This vital information was then sent to the department of water affairs. Satellite technology like this is also used to track climate change like in the Southern Marion islands or map population sizes in cities like Cape Town where urban planning in necessary for growth. Clement: “We are facing a number of socio-economic challenges that requires us to provide crucial information that goes to the extent of saving lives.” SANSAs satellites have been used to track and monitor natural disasters like the Limpopo floods Or the devastation of burn scars left behind by fires, afterwards even the recovery of the vegetation can be monitored. TIMELAPSE 3 SECONDS SANSAs budget is relatively small – only R125 million of this years’ R7.4 billion department budget. But is the information SANSA is providing being used optimally when space technology is so useful? Clement: “I would say to a large extent the data is being used. I’m not sure if the nation is aware to what extent it’s being used.” SANSA wants to inspire the younger generation – people like Anthony - to reach for the skies. Anthony: “The universe, the galaxies, the stars, we need to know them we need to understand what is actually beyond our borders.” He was sent to SANSAs base in Antarctica, an ideal location to study space weather, as it’s where all the Earth’s magnetic field lines converge. Measuring the polarity is integral in understanding how we are protected from the suns solar flares, this information is then sent to SANSAs monitoring lab in Hermanus. Anthony: “That is one highlight of my life! Bongani: “Anthony, we’re black guys, we stay away from places like that.” Anthony: “Hey, Black men cannot survive the cold. I actually wanted to show, hey I’m doing this.” It was a 3 month trip he’ll never forget. Anthony: “It’s a two week voyage to Antarctica, the deep blue sees they keep your seasick the whole time, one night I realized there was no longer darkness outside, we were only seeing light 24.7, and then it was cold! Take your deep freezer and then multiply it by 5-10.” Anthony updated SANSAs space weather monitoring equipment and installed software that will assist the satellites in communicating better with their Hartebeeshoek facility. Gladys hopes research trips like this will inspire our youngsters to become excited about space technology. Bongani: “Why does South Africa need a space agency?” Glays: “We depend a lot on space technology, not only as a country, but as human kind. We are not looking into sending someone to the moon as yet – maybe in the near future.” The unfathomable distances of the unexplored universe make us contemplate our existence. It is a wonderful and immense engine that we still know very little about, and the space technology SANSA is using can only enhance our lives here on earth. PROMO 1: 10 SECONDER Neil Armstrong: “One small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.” WHAT MAKES SOUTH AFRICA’S SPACE AGENCY INTEGRAL TO THE SPACE COMMUNICATION RACE? PROMO 2: 15 SECONDER Gladys: “We are not looking into sending someone to the moon as yet – maybe in the near future.” WHAT MAKES SOUTH AFRICA’S VERY OWN SPACE AGENCY INTEGRAL TO FACILITATING THE TECHNOLOGY THAT KEEPS THE PLANET CONNECTED? PROMO 3: 15 SECONDER SOUTH AFRICA’S VERY OWN SPACE AGENCY FACILITATES GLOBAL COMMUNICATION WITH OUTER SPACE AND ALSO MONITORS NATURAL DISASTERS, GLOBAL WATER SUPPLIES AND CLIMATE CHANGE. MEET OUT SCIENTISTS FUELLING THE FAST-PACED GLOBAL SPACE RACE?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): When you think of space, you think of Russia or America, think again. South Africa has had a space agency for 50yrs and we aren't just looking at the stars, but seeing what space can do for us!
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Gladys Magagula is head of South Africa's mission control room at SANSA (South African Space Agency). She has seen us enter the space race in terms of satellite communication. Because of our prime position relative to space and weather conditions, South Africa is the communications choice for the USA, Russia and China. So much so, we were a part of the Apollo missions securing communication between South Africa and Houston's mission control, we transmitted "One small step for man, one giant leap for mankind." But we have continued and made the space communication race our own. We have sent 3 satellites into space and have had successful launches (from other countries). The information from these is priceless - we can see South Africa in a different way - from weather (droughts etc) and land surveying we can see EVERYTHING from space. So not only are we making money from communicating with satellites for other countries, we are also exploring and making our own satellites.
metadata.Summary: We'll speak to a team of young black researchers who went to Antarctica for SANSA and what they did there and why it's so important to have a "hub" there. We will also interview the head of the weather department Mpho Tshisaphungo - she'll explain operation Phakisa and how we are using the information to accurately forecast unexpected weather - like droughts and floods. They have information dating back 50 years and can spot trends and problems.
